podcast.body: This highly ambitious concept album, envisioned by Rivers Cuomo as Weezer's second record after the "Blue Album," was a space opera intended to have all songs flow into each other without breaks. Developed over much of 1994 and 1995, it featured a narrative of "three dudes, two women and a robot on a mission in space to rescue somebody," serving as an analogy for a new band on tour. The project was eventually abandoned as it "collapsed under its own weight," but later morphed into the "Pinkerton" album. "Rivers Cuomo wanted the second Weezer record to be a space opera. He called it Songs From The Black Hole. This was a concept record with all the songs flowing into each other without breaks. It's very ambitious. After working on it for the better part of a year in 1994 and 1995, it was abandoned. It collapsed under its own weight and never completed and never released."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Unfinished Concept Album
podcast.body: After the success of their 1994 debut record, Rivers Cuomo conceived this science fiction rock opera, set in the year 2126. It featured six characters aboard a spaceship called Bethcy II, exploring a complicated libretto involving a love triangle, a robot, and a baby born in space, all serving as a metaphor for Cuomo's feelings about music business success. He recorded most material at his parents' house over Christmas 1994, with proper recordings made through 1995. The project was abandoned by fall 1995 as Cuomo enrolled at Harvard and band interest waned, leading instead to the *Pinkerton* album. "The whole thing is supposed to be a metaphor for how Rivers felt about success in the music business."

podcast.body: Rivers Cuomo intended this to be a rock opera set in space, a radical departure from *The Blue Album*, where all tracks would form one long composition. The libretto involved Jonas and his shipmates on the spaceship Betsy II with cook Maria, journeying to the stars. Jonas and Maria, who had a history from Starcore Academy, have a baby, and their relationship turns rocky. They land on a planet, encounter a mysterious package, and the story becomes murky. It was an allegory for a new, successful rock band on an uncharted journey. The project collapsed due to the absence of a producer to help sort complex ideas and Rivers's attendance at Harvard, which kept him away from the band for long periods. "Now obviously, Songs from the Black Hole was never released."
